claims.text: Restricting precursor mobility during low-temperature noble-metal HEA nanoparticle formation promotes a stochastic alloying process.
Inhibiting precursor mobility favors formation of a single-phase HEA nanoparticle.
The initial material is a homogeneous, equimolar mixture of single-source precursors for at least five noble metals.
Rapid quenching inhibits precursor mobility during nanoparticle formation.
Slower cooling permits greater precursor mobility than rapid cooling under otherwise identical synthesis conditions.
Mobility inhibition produces a uniform, stochastic distribution of metal atoms within a single phase.
A uniform single-phase elemental distribution establishes optimal dispersion of catalytic active sites.
Limiting precursor mobility minimizes phase separation.
Limiting precursor mobility drives randomized mixing of the constituent metals.
The resulting uniform distribution of active sites enhances catalytic reactions such as the oxygen reduction reaction.
Mobility-inhibited nanoparticles will exhibit more single-phase character than nanoparticles formed with greater precursor mobility.
Mobility-inhibited nanoparticles will have a more uniform elemental distribution than the slower-cooled baseline.
Mobility-inhibited nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than the slower-cooled baseline.
Greater precursor mobility may produce phase separation or a multiphase structure.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies to low-temperature HEA synthesis involving five or more noble metals.
The mechanism may not extend to binary or ternary alloy systems.
The mechanism may not extend to high-temperature syntheses dominated by diffusion-driven processes.
The precise rates of precursor reduction and atomic mixing under mobility-inhibited conditions are not fully quantified.
Solvent environment and precursor-ligand effects may influence HEA formation.
